executive_summary: Wave and tidal energy is no longer uniformly pre-commercial. The sector has split into three distinct investable pathways: behind-the-meter offshore industrial applications where customers already exist, offshore wind co-location plays that avoid transmission cost, and a new wave-plus-AI-data-center model that raised $140 million in May 2026. Northbridge should source deals in the first two categories at Series A/B stage, with the main risk being that utility-scale transmission remains the regulatory default and offshore industrial customer pipelines prove too shallow to support venture returns. The firm's prior 'too early' stance is overtaken by external evidence of go-to-market pivots that sidestep the barriers we originally identified.

market_shifts.description: Wave energy developers are shifting go-to-market strategy from utility-scale grid connection to behind-the-meter offshore industrial customers (oil & gas platforms, aquaculture, sensor networks) because utility procurement timelines are too slow relative to developer burn rates.

Offshore wind developers are beginning to evaluate wave energy as a co-location technology that could share existing offshore substation and transmission infrastructure rather than competing as standalone generation, potentially removing one of wave energy's largest cost disadvantages.

A novel wave energy application combining generation with AI data centers emerged in 2026, with Panthalassa raising $140 million to build floating 'orbs' that pair wave energy generation with onsite AI computing cooled by seawater.

Regulatory progress occurred in the US tidal energy sector, with ORPC filing a draft pilot license application with FERC for an Alaska tidal project in March 2025 and the Cobscook Bay project becoming the first hydrokinetic tidal energy project in the US to gain FERC pilot license approval.

Tribal nation treaty rights emerged as a blocking constraint on tidal energy development in treaty-protected waterways, with Washington State withdrawing a $1.37 million conditional grant for a Puget Sound tidal project in April 2025 after tribal objections.

tensions_or_conflicts: Northbridge's internal view going into the recent industry summit was that wave energy remained pre-commercial and too early for the firm's stage focus (claim 16), but external evidence shows $140 million raised by Panthalassa in May 2026 (claims 0, 1), EUR 32 million Series B1 by CorPower Ocean in October 2024 (claim 2), and Eco Wave Power executing a Nasdaq-listed registered direct offering at a 10.7% premium to market in June 2026 (claim 4) - institutional capital is already deployed at scale, contradicting the 'pre-commercial' characterization.

Northbridge's quarterly sector scan stated that wave/marine energy inbound deal flow remains minimal with fewer than a handful of intros in the most recent quarter (claim 17), yet external evidence shows three significant financing events in 2024-2026 (claims 0, 2, 4) and regulatory progress on FERC pilot licenses (claims 6, 7) - the absence of inbound flow to Northbridge reflects the firm's own positioning rather than sector inactivity.

Northbridge's internal scouting notes explicitly flag offshore co-location economics as the first case heard that meaningfully changes the near-term economics for wave energy and note this was not part of the firm's original thinking (claim 21) - this is the firm's own evidence that its prior 'too early, pre-commercial' stance (claim 16) may now be overtaken, creating internal-to-internal tension between the old default view and new data that contradicts it.

recommendations.text: Initiate outbound sourcing to the unnamed point-absorber wave energy company flagged in internal scouting notes, specifically to understand their behind-the-meter offshore industrial customer pipeline and unit economics when selling directly to oil & gas platforms, aquaculture, or sensor networks rather than utilities. The go-to-market pivot from utility offtake to offshore industrial customers addresses the slow procurement timeline issue that previously made wave energy too early for venture timelines, with the main risk being that the offshore industrial customer base is too fragmented or shallow to support venture-scale outcomes even if individual unit economics work.

Build a target list of wave energy companies pursuing offshore wind co-location strategies, either as turbine suppliers or developer partnerships, to evaluate whether sharing existing offshore substation and transmission infrastructure genuinely removes wave energy's transmission cost disadvantage at commercial scale. This directly addresses the barrier Northbridge originally identified (transmission cost), with the main risk being that offshore wind developers treat co-location as a long-dated option rather than committing capital or offtake agreements in timeframes that match venture fund life.

Track Panthalassa's deployment progress over the next two quarters to determine whether the wave-plus-AI-data-center model achieves technical validation or remains a financing event disconnected from operational reality. A $140 million raise led by Peter Thiel in May 2026 for floating orbs that pair wave energy with onsite AI computing is either a genuine new application or speculative capital chasing narrative, with the main risk being that seawater cooling and wave energy generation each work independently but integrating them in a single floating platform introduces failure modes that kill the combined economics.

Pass on utility-scale wave and tidal energy companies still targeting grid-connected offtake agreements as their primary revenue model, unless they can demonstrate binding utility commitments or regulatory pre-approval that solves the procurement timeline problem. The go-to-market shift to behind-the-meter offshore industrial customers by companies who originally targeted utilities (claim 19) is evidence that utility procurement remains too slow relative to developer burn rate, with the main risk of this pass recommendation being that we miss a company with genuine utility traction in a jurisdiction where procurement has accelerated, but current external evidence (claims 6, 7, 8, 9) shows regulatory process remains multi-year even for pilot licenses.

all_claims.claim: Oregon-based wave energy/AI data center startup Panthalassa raised $140 million in a round led by Peter Thiel, announced around May 4-5, 2026, to build floating 'orbs' that pair wave energy generation with onsite AI computing.
Portland-based Panthalassa's $140 million investment was reported to come from billionaire backers to support development of floating data centers powered by wave energy and cooled by seawater.
CorPower Ocean secured EUR 32 million in Series B1 funding in October 2024, described at the time as the largest single investment in its wave energy technology to date.
A 2026 industry ranking (Naturetechmemos) states CorPower Ocean has raised EUR 95 million in total funding.

Eco Wave Power (Nasdaq: WAVE) announced a $4.0 million registered direct offering of 400,000 ADSs priced at $10.00 each, a 10.7% premium to market, with Maxim Group acting as sole placement agent, announced June 25, 2026.
Eco Wave Power's $4.0 million offering closed on or about June 26, 2026, with proceeds intended to fund global project expansion and AI-driven technology development.
ORPC (Ocean Renewable Power Company) filed a draft pilot license application with FERC for its East Foreland Tidal Energy Project in Cook Inlet, Alaska, reported March 24, 2025.
The Cobscook Bay Tidal Energy Project, after obtaining a FERC pilot license, became the first hydrokinetic tidal energy project within the US to gain such regulatory approval.

The Washington State Department of Commerce withdrew a $1.37 million conditional grant for a proposed tidal energy research project in Puget Sound in response to tribal nation objections over treaty-protected waterways, announced April 4, 2025.
As part of the Rosario Strait Tidal Energy Project public process, September 30, 2025 was the deadline for public comments on the pilot project.
A techno-economic model review states the common target cost for wave energy gradually converges to EUR 0.20/kWh by 2025 and EUR 0.15/kWh (GBP 150/MWh) by 2030.
Nova Innovation was awarded €2.5 million to build an upscaled tidal energy turbine, with a stated tidal energy cost target of €150/MWh by 2025.

Verdant Power states it has received competitive funding awards at the state, federal, and international levels, and conducted in-water testing of its turbine system with total funding of nearly $2.1 million cited on its own site.

A 2025 industry commentary (Alex Epstein) argues that Levelized Cost of Energy (LCOE) as a metric explicitly ignores reliability-related considerations and is criticized as a poor metric for comparing energy sources including renewables like wave.

E2 (Environmental Entrepreneurs) reported that $22 billion in clean energy projects were cancelled in the first half of 2025, including $6.7 billion cancelled in June 2025 alone, with 16,500 jobs lost in 2025 from such cancellations.
Cleanview reports that developers cancelled 1,891 power projects in 2025, with clean energy projects accounting for 93% of all project cancellations that year.

Northbridge has not run formal diligence on any wave energy company to date; its informal prior view, going into a recent industry summit, was that wave energy remained pre-commercial and too early for the firm's stage focus.

Northbridge's quarterly sector scan states that wave/marine energy inbound deal flow remains minimal (fewer than a handful of intros in the most recent quarter), consistent with the firm's internal view that it is one of the least mature sub-segments in advanced energy generation.

Northbridge's scouting notes recorded that renewed wave energy interest at a recent industry summit was increasingly framed around powering offshore infrastructure directly (e.g., oil & gas platforms transitioning to lower-carbon auxiliary power, offshore aquaculture, ocean sensor networks) rather than competing head-to-head with offshore wind for utility-scale generation.

A founder of an unnamed 'point absorber' wave energy design told Northbridge that the company shifted its go-to-market from utility offtake to behind-the-meter offshore industrial customers because utility procurement timelines were too slow relative to the company's burn rate.

An offshore wind developer's business development lead suggested to Northbridge that some larger offshore wind players are watching wave energy as a potential co-location technology (sharing existing offshore substation and transmission infrastructure) rather than as a standalone competing technology, which could remove one of wave energy's biggest cost disadvantages if it materializes.

Northbridge's scouting notes explicitly flag the offshore co-location economics argument as the first case heard that meaningfully changes the near-term economics case for wave energy, since it was not part of the firm's original thinking -- i.e., this is a data point that may overtake the firm's prior 'too early, pre-commercial' stance.

Northbridge's suggested internal follow-up is to hold a scouting call with the unnamed point-absorber wave energy company once they are willing to go on record, specifically to understand their behind-the-meter offshore industrial customer pipeline.

Wave energy remains a small fraction of overall marine/offshore renewable discussion compared to offshore wind, per Northbridge's own scouting observations, even though it came up more in side conversations at the most recent summit than in prior years.
